summary: Explains how a device finds the right Location Information Server (LIS) in its local access network. It defines DHCP options for IPv4 and IPv6 that carry a domain name, which is then resolved through DNS to locate the server. The location itself is then requested from that server with a separate protocol.

eli5.summary: Before you can ask for directions, you must know which information desk to visit. This tells a device how to find the right desk in the network it just joined.

questions: how to discover the location information server
what is a location information server
how does a device discover its lis
subtitle: How a device finds the server in its local network that can tell it where it is.

tldr.problem: A device that wants its location from the network must find the Location Information Server (LIS) that knows the topology of the access network it is currently attached to. Static configuration breaks when the device moves.
tldr.mechanism: New DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options hand the device a domain name for the access network. The device feeds that name into U-NAPTR resolution with the tags LIS and HELD, which returns an HTTP or HTTPS URI for the LIS.
tldr.outcome: The result is a URI usable only for HELD location configuration. HTTPS URIs are authenticated against the domain name that was the input to the process.

today: RFC 5986 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines how a Device finds a LIS for use with HELD (RFC 5985).

sections.title: Why a Device Must Discover Its LIS
sections.content:
A Location Information Server (LIS) uses its knowledge of an access network and its physical topology to generate and serve location information to Devices. Each access network needs specific topology knowledge, so a Device has to find the LIS that serves the network it is on right now. Relying on static configuration can lead to unexpected errors if the Device moves between access networks.

The process uses a DHCP option and the DNS. Its product is an HTTP or HTTPS URI that identifies a LIS. That URI is for location configuration only: the Device MUST dereference it using HELD (RFC 5985). It is not a "location URI", and Devices MUST NOT embed it in fields of other protocols that carry the Device's location.
sections.eli5: If you move to a new building, the information desk is in a different place. Your device needs a way to find the desk in the building it is in now.

sections.title: The Discovery Procedure
sections.content:
The procedure has three steps: acquire the access network domain name, apply U-NAPTR resolution to get a LIS URI, and verify that the LIS can provide location information. The first URI that gets a successful response from the LIS is used. A Device with several network interfaces SHOULD try each interface and stop when a LIS is found on any of them.

A Device MUST support discovery using the access network domain name DHCP option as input to U-NAPTR. If that option is not available, DHCPv4 option 15 is used. Static configuration of a domain name or LIS URI MAY be used, but it may point to a LIS that cannot locate a Device that has moved.

To verify a URI, the Device makes a HELD location request. Any HTTP 200 response containing a HELD response counts as success, including HELD error responses other than notLocatable. If the LIS ever answers notLocatable, the Device MUST continue or restart discovery, and SHOULD NOT send further requests to that LIS until its network attachment changes or it finds a LIS on another interface.
sections.eli5: The device asks the network for the name of the local help desk, looks the desk up, and then checks that it really answers. If it does not, the device tries somewhere else.

sections.title: Residential Gateways and VPNs
sections.content:
In a home network a residential gateway sits between the Device and the access network. If the gateway does not pass on suitable information, Devices behind it cannot discover a LIS. A gateway can help by passing on an access network domain name from the provider, by discovering a LIS on its external interface and giving Devices the domain name that worked, by carrying configuration that names a particular LIS, or by acting as a LIS itself. Configured values stay accurate only while the gateway does not move.

A Device MUST NOT attempt LIS discovery over a VPN interface until it has tried and failed on all other non-VPN interfaces. A LIS found over a VPN is unlikely to know the Device's true location. Because a VPN interface cannot always be detected, a LIS on the far side may be found by accident; the notLocatable error protects the Device from relying on it.
sections.eli5: A home router can pass along the name of the help desk, or be the help desk itself. A device should ask the nearby desk first, not one reached through a long tunnel far away.

sections.title: The Access Network Domain Name Options
sections.content:
The access network domain name is a name owned by the access network operator and meant for discovering services inside that network. It is encoded as in RFC 1035 Section 3.1: each label is a one-octet length followed by that many octets, and the name ends with a zero length byte. The two high bits of every length octet MUST be zero, so a label is at most 63 octets, and the whole encoded name is limited to 255 octets. For example, example.com. takes 13 octets.

The DHCPv4 option is OPTION_V4_ACCESS_DOMAIN with code 213; the DHCPv6 option is OPTION_V6_ACCESS_DOMAIN with code 57. Both carry a single domain name and MUST contain precisely one root label. A DHCPv4 client MAY ask for the option in a Parameter Request List, and a DHCPv6 client in an Options Request Option.

Alternative domain names, for example from static configuration, MAY be tried, but MUST NOT be used unless the access network option is unsuccessful or external information says to use them. Names from other DHCP options, such as the FQDN options, are unlikely to be useful since they are provided without LIS discovery in mind.
sections.eli5: The network hands the device a name tag, like "Springfield Library", written in a special compact way. The device uses that name to look up the help desk.

sections.title: U-NAPTR Resolution of a LIS URI
sections.content:
U-NAPTR (RFC 4848) takes a domain name and produces a URI. Two tags tell DNS which records matter: the Application Service tag LIS and the Application Protocol tag HELD, together written LIS:HELD. The RFC's example delegates two zones to outsource.example.com., whose terminal record with flag u yields https://lis.example.org:4802/?c=ex.

Resolution can give several results, ordered by the NAPTR order and preference values. A Device MAY try alternatives if the first fails, but if a request returns notLocatable or equivalent it SHOULD NOT try other choices from the same domain name.

An HTTPS LIS URI from U-NAPTR MUST be authenticated using the domain name method of RFC 2818 Section 3.1, using the name extracted from the URI, not the one given to U-NAPTR as input.
sections.eli5: Looking up the name in the phone book gives the street address of the help desk. The phone book entry may even say to ask a different office, which then gives the final address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main attack is impersonating a LIS, since location is critical to several network services and a Device may have no prior relationship with the LIS. An attacker could falsify the input domain name, alter the DNS records used in U-NAPTR, or impersonate the LIS itself. The protections described MUST be applied unless similar ones exist, or in cases such as an emergency where location information of dubious origin is arguably better than none.

The name used to authenticate the LIS is the U-NAPTR input, so DNS answers need no integrity protection. Many HTTP clients cannot authenticate against a name other than the one in the request URI, so a client MAY reject URIs whose domain differs from the U-NAPTR input, and administrators SHOULD make the DHCP domain name match the one in the resulting URI.

All of this relies on the integrity of the DHCP domain name, so DHCP messages must be protected from modification or spoofing, for example by physical or link-layer security or DHCP authentication (RFC 3118). A LIS identified by an HTTP URI cannot be authenticated and does not meet the HELD confidentiality and integrity requirements.
sections.eli5: The big danger is a fake help desk giving wrong directions. So the device checks the desk's name tag against the name it started with, and the network must make sure nobody swaps that name.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA assigned DHCPv4 option code 213 and DHCPv6 option code 57 for the access network domain name options. It also registered the U-NAPTR Application Service tag LIS, for a service that provides a Device with its location information, and the Application Protocol tag HELD, applicable to the LIS service with terminal NAPTR record type U. Both name RFC 5986 as the defining publication.
sections.eli5: The official list of names and numbers got new entries, so everyone agrees what the option numbers and the LIS and HELD labels mean.
